title: Pointers, Structures, Memory & Files
intro: Pointers and addresses, structures and unions, dynamic memory allocation, file handling and the preprocessor.

sec.s: When a program runs, its objects occupy storage for particular periods of time.

b.x: When a program runs, its objects occupy storage for particular periods of time. A variable has a type, a value, and an address associated with its storage when it is an object whose address can be taken. An address identifies a location in memory. C lets programs work with addresses through pointers.
For example:

The expression &number means “address of number.” The %p format specifier is used to print a void pointer. The printed address is implementation-dependent; do not expect a specific numeric address or assume that it stays the same between program executions. The important concept is that &number produces a pointer to the object number.

Different variables normally occupy different storage locations when their lifetimes overlap, but do not reason about addresses by guessing how the compiler lays out every object. Compilers may optimize code, place objects in registers when their addresses are not needed, and organize storage in implementation-specific ways. C specifies behavior, not a single universal memory map.
A simplified mental model divides memory use into:

x: Automatic storage, commonly used for local variables and function parameters, whose lifetime is tied to block execution.
Static storage, used by file-scope objects and objects declared static, which exist for the program’s lifetime.
Dynamically allocated storage, obtained through functions such as malloc and released with free.
String literals and other read-only program data, whose exact placement is implementation-dependent and which must not be modified.

b.x: These are useful conceptual categories, not a guarantee that every machine uses a particular physical stack or heap layout. The language rules about lifetime and valid access are more important than the hardware picture.

sec.s: A pointer is an object that stores a pointer value referring to an object or function, or a null…

b.x: A pointer is an object that stores a pointer value referring to an object or function, or a null pointer value. A pointer type indicates what kind of object the pointer can point to when dereferenced.

Here ptr is a pointer to int. The * in the declaration indicates pointer type. The & operator obtains the address of number. The expression *ptr, called dereferencing or indirection, accesses the int object referred to by ptr.

The assignment through ptr modifies number because ptr points to number. The pointer itself is not the same as the pointed-to value. ptr holds an address-like pointer value; ptr refers to the object at that location.
2.1 Null pointers
A null pointer does not point to a valid object. It can be represented with NULL, defined in standard headers, or by a null pointer constant such as 0 in the appropriate context:
Check a pointer before dereferencing it when null is a possible state:

This check protects against a null pointer only. It does not prove that a non-null pointer is valid: it may be dangling, uninitialized, or point to an object whose lifetime has ended. Every pointer used for dereferencing must have a valid target with a suitable lifetime and alignment.
2.2 Uninitialized and dangling pointers
An uninitialized automatic pointer has an indeterminate value. Dereferencing it is unsafe and can cause undefined behavior. Initialize pointers before use, often to NULL when there is no target yet.
A dangling pointer refers to storage that is no longer a valid object for that access. For example, returning the address of a local automatic variable is incorrect:

x: return &local; /* invalid after the function returns */

b.x: The local object’s lifetime ends when the function returns. A caller must not dereference the returned pointer. Alternatives include returning the value, writing into caller-provided storage, or allocating storage dynamically and documenting who must free it.

sec.s: Pointer arithmetic is scaled by the size of the pointed-to type.

b.x: Pointer arithmetic is scaled by the size of the pointed-to type. If ptr is an int pointer to the first element of an array, ptr + 1 points to the next int element, not one byte after the current one.

For an array, values + i points to element i, and *(values + i) is equivalent to values[i]. Pointer arithmetic is only defined within the same array object or one position past its end. A one-past pointer can be formed and used for certain comparisons or iteration, but must not be dereferenced.
A common traversal pattern is:

The end pointer is one past the last element. The loop dereferences current only while it points to a real element. Pointer subtraction is defined for pointers into the same array object (or one past it), and produces the difference in elements, not bytes. The result type is ptrdiff_t from <stddef.h>.

Do not add arbitrary byte counts to an int pointer expecting byte-level movement. If byte-oriented access is genuinely required, unsigned char pointers are commonly used, with careful attention to object representation and aliasing rules. Pointer arithmetic is not general-purpose arithmetic: the pointer must be related to a valid array object.
Pointer comparisons:

x: Equality comparison can be used for compatible pointer values, including checking for NULL.
Relational comparison is meaningful in defined cases, such as pointers within the same array object.
Do not use relational pointer comparisons as a portable way to sort unrelated objects by address.

sec.s: Array names are converted to pointers to their first elements in most expressions.

b.x: Array names are converted to pointers to their first elements in most expressions. This is why:
works without writing &a[0], although both a and &a[0] can be used to obtain a pointer to the first element in the appropriate context.

Important distinction: an array is not a pointer. The array has a fixed size as an object, while a pointer is a separate object that stores a pointer value. The conversion from an array expression to a pointer occurs in most expressions, but not in every context. For example, sizeof a gives the size of the entire array, and &a gives a pointer to the whole array type.

x: printf("%zu\n", sizeof a);       /* size of all three elements */
printf("%zu\n", sizeof a[0]);    /* size of one int element */

b.x: When an array is passed to a function, the parameter is adjusted to a pointer type. The function cannot infer the original array length from that pointer. Pass the length explicitly:

x: void print_array(const int a[], size_t n) {

b.x: The declaration const int a[] means the function will not modify elements through that parameter. It does not make the caller’s array globally immutable; it limits what this function can do through a.
4.1 Pointer indexing
Pointer expressions support array-like indexing:
p[i] is defined in terms of pointer arithmetic and dereferencing. This is useful for understanding arrays, but readable code should use the notation that best communicates intent.
4.2 Array of pointers versus pointer to an array
These declarations are different:

x: int *pointers[5];    /* array of five pointers to int */
int (*pointer)[5];   /* pointer to an array of five int */

b.x: Parentheses matter because [] binds more tightly than unary *. In the first declaration, the array contains pointer objects. In the second, pointer is one pointer that can refer to an entire five-element array. This is a useful example of how C declarations combine operators.
4.3 Multidimensional arrays

For int matrix[3][4], the name matrix usually converts to a pointer to its first row, whose type is int (*)[4], not int . The array is contiguous and row-major. A dynamically allocated int may instead describe an array of pointers to separately allocated rows, which is a different memory layout. Do not pass a normal 2D array to a function expecting int ** unless the representation actually matches.

sec.t: Pointers to Pointers and Const Correctness
sec.s: Here p points to number, and pp points to p.

b.x: A pointer can point to another pointer:

Here p points to number, and pp points to p. *pp produces p; **pp produces number. Pointer-to-pointer types are used when a function needs to update a pointer variable owned by the caller, or when representing arrays of pointers.

For example, a function that allocates memory and returns the pointer through an output parameter might accept int **out. It must define what happens on success and failure and ensure that the caller eventually frees the memory.
const describes access restrictions through a particular expression:

x: const int *p1;       /* pointer to const int */
int *const p2 = &x;  /* const pointer to int */
const int *const p3 = &x; /* const pointer to const int */

b.x: A pointer to const int cannot be used to modify the int through that pointer, although another non-const access path may exist. A const pointer cannot be reassigned after initialization. The combinations serve different purposes.

sec.s: A structure groups related members, possibly of different types, into one compound type.

b.x: A structure groups related members, possibly of different types, into one compound type. It is useful for representing a student, product, date, point, employee, or any entity with several attributes.
Definition:
This defines a structure type, not a variable by itself. Declare variables:
Member access uses the dot operator:
A structure can be initialized at declaration:
The initializer values correspond to the members in declaration order. Designated initializers can make intent clearer in C99 and later:

Structure members have their own types and may include arrays or other structures. A structure’s size may be greater than the sum of member sizes because the implementation can insert padding for alignment. Do not assume that a structure’s memory layout is a simple sum of its fields or use raw byte copying as a portable file format.
6.1 Pointer to a structure

The arrow operator -> accesses a member through a structure pointer. The expression p->roll is equivalent to (p).roll. Parentheses are needed in the latter form because the dot operator binds more tightly than unary .
6.2 Nested structures
A structure can contain another structure as a member:
Access nested members with repeated dot operators:
Nested structures keep related data organized and make types reusable. The Date type can be used in many different structures without duplicating its fields.
6.3 Arrays of structures
An array of structures stores many records of the same structure type:
Access the second student’s name with students[1].name. A loop can process all records:
This is a common way to represent a small in-memory database. For larger or variable-size collections, dynamic allocation may be used, with clear rules for capacity and ownership.
6.4 Structure assignment
Structures of the same compatible type can be assigned as whole values:

The assignment copies the structure members. If a member is an array, its elements are part of the structure value and are copied as part of structure assignment. If a member is a pointer, however, the pointer value is copied, not the pointed-to data. This can create shallow copies where two structures refer to the same dynamically allocated memory. Ownership must be considered before copying structures that contain pointers.

sec.s: A union is a user-defined type in which its members share the same storage.

b.x: A union is a user-defined type in which its members share the same storage. A union can hold a value represented through one member at a time. The size is sufficient for the largest member and is subject to alignment requirements.

If d.integer is assigned, integer is the active member for the intended use. Writing d.decimal afterwards stores a float representation in the same storage and replaces the previous value. Reading a different member from the one most recently written requires careful understanding of the C rules and implementation representation; do not treat a union as a safe automatic conversion between unrelated types.
7.1 Structure versus union

A structure allocates storage for all members, with possible padding. A union overlays members in the same storage. Structures are suitable when all fields must exist together, such as a student’s roll, name, and marks. Unions are suitable when a value may be one of several alternative types and saving space or representing variants is important.
Example conceptual variant:
The kind field records which union member is intended to be active. This pattern is sometimes called a tagged union. The program must keep the tag and the actual member in agreement.
7.2 Arrays of unions and pointers to unions
Unions can be elements of arrays and can be pointed to like other object types:
The pointer’s type determines how the selected member is accessed, but the program remains responsible for tracking which member is meaningful.

sec.s: Dynamic memory allocation obtains storage while the program is running, rather than declaring every…

b.x: Dynamic memory allocation obtains storage while the program is running, rather than declaring every object with a fixed automatic array size. The standard functions are declared in <stdlib.h>:

x: malloc: allocates a block of bytes without initializing them.
calloc: allocates space for an array and initializes all bytes to zero.
realloc: changes the size of an existing allocated block, potentially moving it.
free: releases a block previously allocated by a compatible allocation function.

b.x: Dynamic allocation is useful when the amount of data is only known at runtime, when an object must outlive a function’s automatic local variables, or when building structures such as linked lists and trees. It introduces responsibility: every successful allocation must have a clear ownership and release plan.
8.1 malloc

malloc returns a pointer to allocated storage or NULL if allocation fails. The allocated bytes are uninitialized. The expression sizeof values is often preferable to sizeof(int) because it remains correct if the pointer type changes. In C, converting void to an object pointer type is implicit, so a cast is not required for malloc’s result.

The multiplication used to calculate allocation size can overflow for large counts. For externally supplied counts, validate the count and ensure the product is representable before allocating. A successful allocation does not mean the program can safely access more elements than it requested.
8.2 calloc

calloc takes the element count and the size of each element separately. It initializes the allocated bytes to all-bits-zero. For ordinary integer types, this corresponds to integer zero. In strict C language terms, all-bits-zero is not guaranteed to be the representation of every possible floating-point zero or null pointer representation, so do not generalize beyond the documented byte initialization guarantee. Check for NULL before use.
8.3 realloc
realloc changes the size of a previously allocated block:

x: /* values remains valid when new size is nonzero */
/* handle failure without losing the original pointer */

b.x: Use a temporary pointer. If realloc fails for a nonzero requested size, it returns NULL and the original allocation remains valid. Writing “values = realloc(values, …)” directly can lose the original pointer on failure, causing a memory leak. If realloc succeeds, the returned pointer must be used; the block may have moved, and the old pointer is no longer valid for accessing the allocation.

The special case of realloc(ptr, 0) has historically had tricky and standard-version-dependent details. For clear code, handle a desired size of zero by explicitly freeing the block and setting the pointer to NULL rather than relying on realloc with a zero size.
8.4 free

free releases storage obtained from a compatible allocation function. Passing NULL is safe and does nothing. Freeing the same allocation twice, freeing a pointer that was not returned by an allocation function, or using a pointer after free can cause undefined behavior. Setting a local pointer to NULL after free helps avoid accidentally reusing that same pointer variable, but it does not clear copies of the pointer stored elsewhere.
8.5 Complete dynamic array example

The memory remains allocated until free is called or the process terminates. In long-running programs, leaks can accumulate and exhaust memory. Define who owns allocated storage, who may modify it, and who releases it. Avoid returning a pointer to memory that has already been freed.

sec.s: File handling allows a program to store data persistently or read information created by another…

b.x: File handling allows a program to store data persistently or read information created by another program. The standard I/O interface is declared in <stdio.h>. A FILE object represents an open stream; programs usually work with a FILE pointer, such as FILE *fp.
The usual file workflow is:

x: Read from or write to the stream.
Check relevant return values and errors.

b.x: Always check fopen:

A file may fail to open because it does not exist, permissions deny access, the path is wrong, or the operating environment has another error. perror prints a message associated with the current error indicator, where applicable.
9.1 File modes
Common fopen modes:

x: “r”: open an existing text file for reading.
“w”: open for writing; create if needed and truncate an existing file.
“a”: open for appending; create if needed.
“r+”: open an existing file for reading and writing.
“w+”: open for reading and writing, truncating or creating.
“a+”: open for reading and appending, creating if needed.
Add “b” for binary mode where relevant, such as “rb” or “wb”.

b.x: On systems that distinguish text and binary streams, this affects translation rules.
Choose modes carefully. “w” destroys existing file contents by truncating the file. Use “a” when new output should be added at the end. Use “r” when the program must not create a missing file.
9.2 Writing formatted text

fprintf works like printf but sends formatted output to a stream. A successful write can still encounter a later failure when buffered data is flushed, so checking fclose is useful when output integrity matters.
9.3 Reading formatted text

The loop processes successfully parsed integers. When fscanf stops, it may have reached end-of-file or encountered invalid input. ferror checks whether a stream error occurred; feof can test the end-of-file indicator. Do not write while (!feof(fp)) as a general input loop, because the end-of-file indicator is usually set only after a read attempts to go past the end. Instead, test the read function’s return value.
9.4 Character and line input
fgetc reads one character as an int so it can represent every unsigned-char value plus the special EOF value:
Using char for the result can confuse a valid byte with EOF. fgets reads a bounded line into a character buffer:
fputs writes a string to a stream without adding a newline automatically. fgets may include the newline if it fits into the buffer.

sec.s: Sequential access processes data in order, from the current position onward.

b.x: Sequential access processes data in order, from the current position onward. Text line processing and log-file reading commonly use sequential access. It is simple and suitable when every record must be examined.

Random access moves to a particular file position so the program can read or write at that location. Standard C provides fseek, ftell, and rewind for positioning and querying file positions, subject to stream restrictions.

SEEK_SET means an offset from the beginning; SEEK_CUR means an offset from the current position; SEEK_END means an offset from the end, subject to the rules for the stream. ftell returns a long value representing the current file position where supported, or -1L on failure. rewind moves to the start and clears the stream error indicator.
For a fixed-size binary record, random access can be computed when the representation and file format are deliberately designed:

This simple calculation has limits: the multiplication and conversion to long must be valid, and raw structure representations are not portable across compilers or machines because padding, endianness, and type sizes may differ. A robust persistent file format specifies field widths and encoding.

Sequential access is usually easiest for text files and variable-length records. Random access is useful for fixed-size records, indexes, and binary formats designed for seeking. Not every stream is seekable; pipes and some device streams may not support random access.

sec.s: The preprocessor runs before the compiler proper.

b.x: The preprocessor runs before the compiler proper. Preprocessor directives begin with # and are used for including headers, defining macros, conditional compilation, and other source transformations. They are not ordinary C statements and do not end with a semicolon unless the semicolon is part of the replacement text or another relevant construct.
11.1 #include

Angle brackets conventionally search implementation-defined system include locations. Double quotes conventionally search the local or project-specific locations first, then other configured locations. Exact search behavior is compiler-dependent. Include headers for the functions and types used.
11.2 #define
A simple object-like macro:
The preprocessor replaces occurrences of the macro name with its replacement tokens. A function-like macro:
Parentheses are important, but even this macro can evaluate its argument more than once. SQUARE(i++) is unsafe because i++ appears twice. For ordinary calculations, prefer a function:
Macros are textual substitutions, not type-checked functions. Avoid macros when a const object, enum constant, or function communicates the intention more safely.
11.3 Include guards
A header can be included through multiple paths. Include guards prevent its contents from being processed repeatedly in one translation unit:
The macro name should be unique to the header. Many compilers also support #pragma once, but traditional include guards are portable standard practice.
11.4 Conditional compilation

Other directives include #if, #elif, #else, #endif, #ifndef, #undef, and #error. Conditional compilation can select platform-specific code or enable debugging output. It should not be confused with runtime if statements: preprocessing happens before the program runs.
11.5 Predefined macros

Common predefined macros include FILE and LINE, which expand to source file and line information, and DATE and TIME in many standard implementations. These can help with diagnostics but should not be used as security guarantees. The exact set of predefined macros depends on the C standard and implementation.

sec.s: Where supported, address and undefined-behavior sanitizers can help find memory errors during…

b.x: Pointer errors:

x: Dereferencing NULL or an uninitialized pointer.
Returning a pointer to a local variable.
Dereferencing a dangling pointer after free.
Using pointer arithmetic outside an array object.
Treating an int ** as interchangeable with a pointer to a 2D array.
Forgetting that pointer arithmetic is scaled by the pointed-to type.

b.x: Structure and union errors:

x: Forgetting the struct keyword when no typedef exists.
Using . instead of -> for a pointer to a structure.
Assuming structure members are laid out without padding.
Assuming copying a structure deep-copies memory pointed to by its members.
Reading a union member without tracking which value is intended to be active.

b.x: Dynamic memory errors:

x: Not checking malloc or calloc for NULL.
Allocating the wrong number of bytes.
Multiplication overflow in allocation size calculations.
Losing the original pointer when realloc fails.

b.x: File errors:

x: Using “w” when existing contents should be preserved.
Ignoring read or write return values.
Using while (!feof(file)) instead of checking the read operation.
Assuming raw structure bytes are a portable file format.

b.x: Preprocessor errors:

x: Using macro arguments that have side effects.
Assuming a preprocessor #if is a runtime condition.
Defining generic macro names that collide with identifiers elsewhere.

b.x: Compile with warnings:

Where supported, address and undefined-behavior sanitizers can help find memory errors during testing. Test failure paths as well as success paths: simulate allocation failure where practical, try missing files, test empty files, and verify that cleanup occurs on every error path.

sec.s: Pointers are powerful because they allow indirect access to objects, but their correctness depends…

b.x: Pointers are powerful because they allow indirect access to objects, but their correctness depends on lifetime and ownership. A pointer does not keep its target alive. If a local object goes out of scope or a dynamic allocation is freed, any pointer that still refers to that storage must not be used to access it.

A practical ownership rule is: for every allocated block, identify one responsible owner that will eventually release it. Other pointers may be temporary non-owning references, but they must not outlive the allocation. When ownership is transferred to another function, document whether the caller remains responsible for freeing the block or whether the callee takes responsibility.

For example, a function that receives int *values and a length may only borrow the array and must not call free(values), unless its contract explicitly says ownership is transferred. Conversely, a function that returns a newly allocated block should clearly document that the caller must free it.

A pointer should be initialized before it is used. NULL is a useful initial state for a pointer that has no target. After freeing a block, assigning the owning pointer to NULL reduces the chance of accidental reuse, but it cannot fix aliases held by other variables. Those aliases become dangling pointers too.

Avoid using pointers to objects with shorter lifetimes than the pointer's intended use. Do not store the address of a function's local variable in a global pointer and expect it to remain valid after the function returns. Use caller-provided output storage, static storage where appropriate, or dynamic allocation with a clear release policy.

sec.t: More Pointer Arithmetic and Array Layout
sec.s: Pointer arithmetic is based on elements, not bytes.

b.x: Pointer arithmetic is based on elements, not bytes. If int *p points to the first element of an int array, p + 2 points to the third element. If char *c points into a character array, c + 2 points two char elements ahead. The compiler uses the pointed-to type to scale the offset.
For an array of five integers:
The half-open range [begin, end) contains the five elements. The end pointer points one past the final element. This convention makes loops and ranges easy to express:

The pointer end must not be dereferenced. Forming it is permitted because it is exactly one past the same array. A pointer beyond that position is not valid to form through ordinary pointer arithmetic.
The relation between arrays and pointers also explains why this is valid:
The left side uses array indexing; the right side adds i elements to the pointer and dereferences the result. Both require a valid index. Pointer syntax does not bypass array bounds rules.
For a 2D array:

the row size is sizeof grid[0], and the address of grid + 1 advances by one whole row. The expression grid decays to a pointer to an array of four int, not to int **. This is why a function that accepts int grid[][4] can access rows correctly, while an int ** parameter describes a different layout.

sec.s: Structure members are declared in order, but a compiler may insert padding between members or at…

b.x: Structure members are declared in order, but a compiler may insert padding between members or at the end to satisfy alignment requirements. For example:

The sizeof the structure may be larger than sizeof(char) + sizeof(int) + sizeof(char). The exact size depends on the implementation's type sizes and alignment rules. Use sizeof(struct Example) rather than assuming a byte count.

Padding is not necessarily wasteful; it can allow the processor to access members efficiently. Reordering members may reduce padding on a particular implementation, but do not change a public data layout casually, and do not rely on one compiler's layout when exchanging binary data between systems.

Structure assignment copies the members as values. If a structure contains a pointer to dynamically allocated data, the pointer value is copied but the allocation is not duplicated. This is called a shallow copy. If both copies are treated as owners and both free the same allocation, a double-free bug can result. A deep copy must allocate and copy the pointed-to data separately.
A structure can contain another structure, an array, or a pointer to its own type. Self-referential structures are used for linked lists and trees:

The pointer member can refer to another Node. The structure cannot contain a full instance of itself directly because that would require infinite size, but a pointer has a known size and can refer to another object of that type.

sec.s: A union overlays its members in shared storage.

b.x: A union overlays its members in shared storage. It is useful when a program needs to represent one of several alternative forms. A tagged union stores an enum or other tag alongside the union so the program can remember which member is meaningful.

When kind is KIND_INT, code should read value.i; when kind is KIND_FLOAT, code should read value.f. Every update should keep the tag and union member consistent. If the tag says integer but the code reads the float member, the program may interpret the same bytes in an unintended way.

Unions are sometimes used in low-level programming, protocol parsing, and memory-conscious data structures. They are not a general-purpose way to convert a number from one type to another. Converting a numeric value should normally use a normal assignment or cast. Reinterpreting the stored representation is a different operation and has portability constraints.

sec.s: Dynamic memory management has four stages: request storage, check success, use only the requested…

b.x: Dynamic memory management has four stages: request storage, check success, use only the requested region, and release it when finished. The allocated object's lifetime begins when allocation succeeds and ends when the block is released or reallocated in a way that replaces the block.
Example with a dynamically sized array:

The count should be checked before multiplying it by element size, especially if n comes from user input. If the multiplication overflows size_t, the allocation request may be smaller than intended. Robust code can check whether n > SIZE_MAX / sizeof *data before multiplying, with SIZE_MAX available from <stdint.h> on implementations that provide it.

malloc returns uninitialized storage. calloc initializes all bytes to zero, but it should not be described as calling a constructor or performing arbitrary semantic initialization. realloc may move the allocation and preserves the existing contents up to the smaller of the old and new sizes. If it succeeds, the returned pointer is the one to use. If it fails for a nonzero request, the old allocation remains valid.

Never call free twice on the same allocation. A good cleanup strategy is to initialize owning pointers to NULL, use a single cleanup path when a function has several resources, and release every resource that was successfully acquired. free(NULL) is safe, which can simplify cleanup. Do not access memory after free, even if the old bytes appear unchanged.

sec.t: File Handling: Text and Binary Data
sec.s: Text files store character representations intended to be interpreted as text.

b.x: Text files store character representations intended to be interpreted as text. Examples include configuration files, CSV data, and logs. Binary files store bytes according to a defined representation. The terms “text” and “binary” can have different platform details, especially where text streams translate newline conventions.

Formatted functions such as fprintf and fscanf interpret values according to format strings. Character functions such as fgetc and fputc process one character at a time. Line functions such as fgets and fputs process strings. Binary functions fread and fwrite transfer blocks of bytes.
Example writing an array of integers in binary form:

x: size_t written = fwrite(values, sizeof values[0], count, fp);

b.x: Example reading records:

x: size_t read_count = fread(values, sizeof values[0], capacity, fp);
/* read_count tells how many complete elements were read */

b.x: The count returned by fread or fwrite is the number of complete elements, not necessarily the number of bytes. Always check the result. A short read may mean end-of-file or an error, so use feof and ferror as appropriate.

Writing a raw structure with fwrite may be convenient for a program that reads the file on the same implementation, but it is not automatically a portable storage format. Structure padding, byte order, integer widths, and floating-point representations can differ. For long-lived or shared files, define a format explicitly, such as text fields or a binary protocol with specified widths and byte order.
21.1 Sequential access

Sequential processing reads records in order. It is natural for a CSV file, a text report, or a log. A loop checks the return value of the input function and processes each successfully read record. Do not use feof as the loop's only condition because the end-of-file indicator is generally set only after a read attempt reaches the end.
21.2 Random access

fseek changes the file position for streams that support seeking. ftell can report the current position, and rewind returns to the beginning. Random access is useful for fixed-size records or indexes, but the position calculation must be valid and the stream must support it. Text streams have additional restrictions on permitted offsets; portable code should not assume arbitrary byte offsets are meaningful in every text file.
21.3 Closing and error handling

fclose flushes buffered output and releases the stream. If output matters, check whether fclose returns EOF. A write may appear to succeed because data was buffered, then fail during flush or close. Close files on all paths, including after errors, and do not use a FILE pointer after fclose.

sec.s: Preprocessing is a source-transformation stage that runs before normal C compilation.

b.x: Preprocessing is a source-transformation stage that runs before normal C compilation. Directives begin with # and are processed according to preprocessor rules. They are not runtime commands.

#include makes declarations and definitions from a header available to the translation unit. A header such as stdio.h declares standard input/output functions; string.h declares string functions; stdlib.h declares dynamic memory and conversion functions. Include the correct header rather than manually inventing function declarations.

#define creates a macro. Object-like macros replace a name with a token sequence. Function-like macros accept arguments and expand textually. Always parenthesize macro parameters and the overall replacement expression where needed:

Even with parentheses, a macro may evaluate an argument multiple times. For example, ADD(i++, 1) evaluates i++ once, but a macro like SQUARE(i++) can evaluate it twice. Use functions for operations that require normal single-evaluation semantics.
Include guards prevent a header's contents from being processed multiple times in a single translation unit:

Conditional compilation uses #if, #ifdef, #ifndef, #elif, #else, and #endif. It can select code based on compile-time macros. This differs from an if statement, which is part of the compiled program and chooses a path at runtime. #error can deliberately stop preprocessing with a diagnostic. #undef removes a macro definition.

Macros should have specific names to avoid collisions. A macro can replace tokens in places where a programmer does not expect, because the preprocessor does not understand ordinary C scope in the same way the compiler does. Prefer constants, enums, and functions when they provide clearer semantics.

sec.s: Key ideas and examples

x: 1. Why is it unsafe to dereference an uninitialized pointer?
Its value is indeterminate and may not point to a valid object.
2. What does p + 1 mean for int *p?
A pointer one int element after p, when the operation is within the same array object or one past its end.
3. Can a pointer to a 2D array be treated as int **?
No. A normal 2D array is laid out as an array of rows; int ** describes a pointer to a pointer and commonly has a different layout.
4. Why can a structure be larger than the sum of its members?
The implementation may insert padding for alignment.
5. What is a shallow copy of a structure containing a pointer?
The pointer value is copied, but the pointed-to allocation is not.
6. Why use a tag with a union?
It records which union member the program intends to treat as active.
7. What is the difference between malloc and calloc?
malloc allocates uninitialized bytes; calloc allocates an array-like block and initializes all bytes to zero.
8. Why is direct assignment from realloc risky?
On failure for a nonzero size, the old allocation remains valid; direct assignment can lose the only pointer to it.
It closes the stream and flushes pending output where applicable; its return value should be checked when errors matter.
It changes a stream's file position when the stream supports seeking.
11. What is the difference between #if and if?
#if is processed before compilation; if is a runtime control statement.
They are textual substitutions and may evaluate arguments multiple times or interact unexpectedly with surrounding expressions.

sec.s: Addresses and pointers: know &, *, pointer declarations, NULL, pointer arithmetic, array bounds…

b.x: Addresses and pointers: know &, *, pointer declarations, NULL, pointer arithmetic, array bounds, pointer lifetime, and dangling pointers.
Arrays: know how array names convert to pointers, why a 2D array is not automatically an int **, and how to pass lengths explicitly.
Structures: know definition, initialization, dot and arrow access, nested structures, arrays of structures, padding, and shallow copying.
Unions: know shared storage, the active-member idea, tagged unions, and the difference between a union and a structure.
Dynamic memory: know malloc, calloc, realloc, and free; check allocation results; prevent size overflow; avoid leaks, double frees, and use-after-free.
Files: know fopen modes, return-value checking, formatted and character I/O, fread/fwrite, sequential access, fseek/ftell/rewind, and fclose.
Preprocessor: know #include, #define, include guards, conditional compilation, and the difference between compile-time preprocessing and runtime logic.

Practice small programs and trace every pointer, index, allocation, file position, and error path. C gives the programmer substantial control, but it does not automatically enforce bounds, ownership, or correct resource management.

sec.s: This example writes a few records as readable text.

b.x: This example writes a few records as readable text. It demonstrates a structure, an array of structures, fopen, fprintf, error checking, and fclose. Text files are easier to inspect manually than raw binary files.

x: size_t count = sizeof students / sizeof students[0];

b.x: The file is written in a simple comma-separated format. This example assumes names do not contain commas or newlines; a true CSV implementation must define quoting and escaping rules. The "w" mode truncates any existing students.txt file, so use another mode if preserving existing content is required.

A reader could open the file with "r" and use a carefully designed parser. Using fscanf with "%d,%29[^,],%f" may work for this simple restricted format, but parsing general CSV is more complex because quoted fields can contain commas, quotes, and line breaks. A robust parser should follow the actual file format specification instead of assuming every comma separates a field.

sec.t: Mini Project: Dynamically Growing A Collection
sec.s: A program may not know the number of records in advance.

b.x: A program may not know the number of records in advance. One design is to allocate an initial capacity and grow it when the logical length reaches capacity. The logical length is how many elements are currently stored; capacity is how many elements can fit without allocating again.
Before using the pointer, check for allocation failure. When length equals capacity, compute a larger capacity and call realloc through a temporary pointer:

x: /* Keep values and capacity unchanged; report failure. */

b.x: Only after successful reallocation should the program update its pointer and capacity. It can then write values[length] and increment length. A complete implementation must also guard against capacity multiplication overflow and against overflow in new_capacity * sizeof *values. The doubling strategy makes appending efficient on average, but it is a design choice, not a language requirement.

At the end, free the allocation exactly once. If an operation fails midway, the cleanup path must still release any block that was successfully allocated. This pattern is a foundation for implementing a dynamic array, though a reusable library should package pointer, length, and capacity together in a structure and document its functions.

sec.s: Consider a program that reads a file one character at a time.

b.x: Consider a program that reads a file one character at a time. fgetc returns the next character converted to int, or EOF when no character can be read. The program should distinguish ordinary end-of-file from an input error after the loop:

This is safer than checking feof before attempting to read. Before the read attempt that reaches the end, the end-of-file indicator may not yet be set. The read result itself tells the loop when to stop.

For random access, remember that fseek's offset and origin work together. SEEK_SET is relative to the beginning; SEEK_CUR is relative to the current position; SEEK_END is relative to the end where the stream and operation support it. Check fseek's return value. ftell may fail and return -1L, so do not blindly cast its result to an unsigned type. Large files and platform extensions may need more capable position APIs, but those are not part of the most basic portable C interface.

Text streams can restrict which offsets are valid. For binary streams, the file-position model is closer to byte offsets, but portability still depends on the data format. A file position is not a database index: it is a location within the stream and does not itself identify a logical record unless the program's file format defines the relationship.

sec.s: Before dereferencing a pointer, ask: Was it initialized?

b.x: Before dereferencing a pointer, ask: Was it initialized? Does it point to a live object? Is the object the expected type? Is the access within its bounds? Does the pointer have correct alignment? If it points to dynamic storage, has that storage already been freed?

Before allocating memory, ask: Is the element count valid? Can count times element size overflow? Did allocation succeed? Who owns the block? Which code path releases it? What happens if the next allocation fails?

Before using a structure, ask: Is the type definition visible? Is member access using . or -> correctly? Are pointers inside the structure initialized? Would a structure assignment create shared ownership of a pointer target?
Before using a union, ask: Which member is intended to be active? Is a tag available? Does every update keep the tag consistent with the data?

Before using a file, ask: Did fopen succeed? Is the mode appropriate? Does the input loop check the read result? Are writes checked? Does the code distinguish EOF from error? Is fclose called on success and failure paths? Can the stream seek? Is the stored format portable enough for its purpose?

Before using macros, ask: Would a function be clearer? Are arguments evaluated more than once? Are replacement expressions parenthesized? Is the macro name specific? Does the include guard match the header?

These questions turn C debugging into a systematic process rather than guesswork. Compiler warnings, small test files, sanitizers where available, and careful tracing are useful tools, but they do not replace understanding the language's rules.
